content: Receptive information and services related to contraception must be provided without discrimination, coercion, or violence. Every individual has the right to privacy and confidentiality when receiving contraceptive information and services. Adolescents must have access to post-abortion contraceptive information and services without requiring parental or guardian authorization. States must ensure that practices of conscientious refusal or objection do not infringe upon the right to access contraceptive information and services. Abortion care services can be delivered by a variety of health workers, and some tasks can be managed by individuals themselves. For example, pre-abortion information and counseling, cervical priming, or post-abortion follow-up care can occur in different locations. Unlike surgical abortion, medical abortion is a process that unfolds over several hours or days rather than being a single, discrete procedure. This process, or its components, can take place in various settings, including self-management or with the support of health workers at different stages, allowing for care to be obtained in a range of settings and through diverse options. Medical abortion services can be provided or supported by multiple actors within the health system. These services may be delivered through comprehensive models addressing the full spectrum of abortion care or may focus on specific components of the care pathway. Services can be offered through public or private sectors, non-governmental organizations (NGOs), community-based locations, off-site facilities, or even at home. A variety of service delivery models can coexist at national, subnational, and local levels. As digital technologies advance and evidence on effective interventions evolves, innovations in service delivery will continue to develop. Examples of service delivery approaches include: 1. Accompaniment models: Community health workers provide support during the medical abortion process, offering information, counseling, emotional or logistical support, and referrals to local healthcare facilities if needed. 2. Community outreach: Health workers are mobilized to provide services in remote or rural areas, such as through mobile clinics, though evidence on this model for abortion care is limited. 3. Digital support tools: Apps and platforms provide information, reminders, and tools to assist in assessing pregnancy duration. 4. Harm reduction models: Women are supported with pre-abortion information, guidance on obtaining and using medications, and post-abortion support, but the medications themselves are not provided. 5. Hotlines: Telephone-based information services support women in accessing quality abortion care, providing evidence-based information or linking to other service delivery models. 6. Social marketing: Marketing techniques are applied to promote access to abortion medicines and instructions, aiming to increase affordability and accessibility. 7. Social franchising: NGOs use commercial franchise structures to achieve social goals, focusing on providing safe and accessible abortion care. Interactions between abortion seekers and health workers can occur in person or remotely. Telemedicine approaches are recommended as an alternative to in-person interactions for delivering medical abortion services, including eligibility assessment, counseling, medication administration, and follow-up care. Evidence supports the use of telemedicine for medical abortion, showing no significant differences in outcomes compared to in-person care, with high satisfaction rates reported. Self-management of medical abortion is a viable option for pregnancies under 12 weeks, using either mifepristone plus misoprostol or misoprostol alone. Women can self-assess eligibility, self-administer abortion medications, and evaluate the success of the abortion process outside of healthcare facilities and without direct supervision. However, individuals must have access to accurate information, quality-assured medications, trained health worker support, and referral services if needed. Regulatory frameworks may need to adapt to facilitate self-management within health systems. Service delivery approaches should be co-created with the intended beneficiaries, tested and adapted for local contexts, and monitored for quality and accountability. States must ensure that sexual and reproductive health services are available, accessible, affordable, acceptable, and of good quality, respecting cultural, gender, age, and other diversities. Accurate, evidence-based abortion information must be provided confidentially, and services must be delivered without discrimination, ensuring access to modern and safe contraceptive methods and abortion medicines.
